pronunciation.ipaLabel: Conventional reading — Egyptian vocalisation not attested

phonemes.desc: Written gb; the g is a voiced velar stop, the b a voiced bilabial. Conventionally vocalised “Geb”.
Final b consonantal; the goose-determinative often accompanies the name.

pronunciation.note: The goose (gb) is both his sacred animal and a pun on his name — “the Cackler”. The name is among the shortest in the Egyptian pantheon.

domains.title: God of the Earth, Its Riches and Its Snakes
domains.subtitle: The Laughing Earth Beneath the Sky
domains.lead: Gb — Geb — is the earth itself as a god: the ground that yields gold and grain, the floor of the world, and father of the third generation of the gods. He lies beneath his sister-wife Nut, parted from her by Shu, and his laughter is the tremor in the ground — the Egyptians heard earthquakes as the earth-god laughing.

cards.name: The Earth God
cards.desc: The soil, the mines, the buried treasure: everything underfoot is his body and his property.

cards.name: The Cackler
cards.desc: His sacred goose gives him the epithet “the Cackler”; his cry was the world’s first sound in some cosmogonies.

cards.name: Father of the Ennead
cards.desc: By Nut he fathered Osiris, Isis, Seth, Nephthys, Horus the Elder — the gods whose quarrels drive Egyptian myth.

cards.name: Judge of the Divine Tribunal
cards.desc: He presides over the council of gods in the succession myth of Horus and Seth.

mythology.lead: Geb’s mythology is the deep structure under the Osiris cycle: the separation of earth and sky that creates the world’s space, and the divine tribunal over which he presides when Horus and Seth dispute the succession. His jealousy of Osiris — in one strand he lies with Nut and fathers the five gods on the forbidden days — is the genealogical knot of the whole pantheon.

myths.title: Parted from Nut
myths.text: Born of Shu and Tefnut, Geb and Nut loved without space between them until Shu, on Ra’s command, wrenched them apart — and the world’s breathable distance dates from that separation. Geb’s green fertility and Nut’s starry vault remain arched apart for eternity, the air god’s arms the only thing between them.

myths.title: The Five Children on the Epagomenal Days
myths.text: Though the birth of the five gods belongs to Nut’s myth, the Pyramid Texts address Geb as their father and as the mountain of the west on which the dead king ascends. ‘You are Geb, the heir of the gods,’ the utterances tell the king — the earth is the ultimate estate of succession.

myths.title: The Tribunal of Geb
myths.text: In the New Kingdom narrative of the divine lawsuit, the gods weary of the eighty-year dispute between Horus and Seth and appeal to Geb, who as earth and eldest remaining power hears the case and awards the Two Lands to Horus, assigning Seth to the desert and the thunder — the judicial myth behind the division of the living king from the dangerous margins.

myths.title: The Earth Receives the Dead
myths.text: Spell 125’s negative confession addresses the earth directly — ‘I have not polluted the soil’ — because the soil is Geb’s body and the dead enter it as guests. The grave itself, the shaft and chamber, is a doorway into the god; to be buried was literally to be taken into Geb.

lore.syncretism: The Greeks identified Geb with their own earth — Cronos in the common equation, which made mythographic sense of his fatherhood of the divine generation. Through Plutarch this mapping circulated widely, though Egyptian theology itself kept him younger and more fertile than the aged Titan. Roman-period underworld iconography occasionally fuses his image with that of the infernal judge.
lore.culturalLegacy: Geb is less famous than his children but structurally indispensable: every genealogy of the Egyptian gods runs through him. His laughter-as-earthquake remains one of the most charming etiological fragments of Egyptian religion, quoted in every handbook; and his goose still cackles on temple walls at Kom Ombo and Esna.
lore.extendedMeditation: Two letters — gb — hold up the whole world. The restoration is a consonant-pair, and the goose beside it in the hieroglyphic spelling is the vowel the Egyptians did not write. This temple’s name is the shortest in the pantheon, and the heaviest: it is the ground beneath every other name in the lexicon.

sources.name: Pyramid Texts (Geb as father and throne-estate)
Contendings of Horus and Seth (New Kingdom narrative)
Book of the Dead, spell 125 (confession to the earth)
Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (Greek identifications)

lore.archaeology: Geb appears wherever the earth needs a face: relief programmes at Kom Ombo and Esna show him green-skinned with the goose; the second hypostyle of Karnak’s Khonsu temple and the Barque shrine of Luxor preserve fine Green-God imagery. His goose emblem anchors the corners of temple floor-plans as the four corners of the earth.
lore.cult: No major city was exclusively his — the earth cannot have one owner — but he received regular offering as ‘the house of Geb’ wherever ground was broken, and the royal accession rites included the new king’s enthronement ‘upon the throne of Geb’, the earth itself as the seat of legitimacy.
lore.iconography: A man of green skin and goose-head or with the goose upon his head, lying beneath the arched Nut; in judgement scenes he is seated as president of the divine council. His laughter, when shown, is the hieroglyph of the goose with open beak — the cackle written into his name.
lore.reception: Classical syncretism as Cronos gave him an afterlife in Plutarch and the Hermetica; modern Egyptology treats him as the canonical earth-god of the Ennead and the clearest demonstration of Egyptian theological literalism — the earth is not like a god, it is one.
